relations.subject: vector-search:nlist
relations.evidence: For Composite Vector indexes, tests show that increasing `nList` beyond the default does not affect the build time of the index. However, it does improve the queries per second (QPS) that the index can handle.

relations.subject: vector-search:nlist
relations.evidence: Hyperscale Vector indexes tend to perform better with larger centroids (smaller `nList` values).

relations.subject: index-type:composite-vector
relations.evidence: Most of the tests were performed using the Hyperscale Vector index. However, many of the results also apply to Composite Vector indexes where the two index types share the same settings.

relations.subject: vector-search:nprobes
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - tradesOffAgainst. Reason: this page is dominated by explicit speed/accuracy/memory tradeoff statements (increase X, get more accuracy but lower QPS/higher latency) that don't fit mustUseInsteadWhen (not a substitution) or behavesDifferentlyUnder (not an index-type contrast); no promoted predicate captures a graduated cost/benefit knob.
relations.evidence: Tests show that increasing `nProbes` beyond the default improves the accuracy of results non-linearly (larger values show diminishing improvements). However, it caused a linear decrease in QPS and increase in latency.

relations.subject: vector-search:reranking
relations.evidence: Testing shows that enabling reranking improves the accuracy of recall in limited cases and decreases QPS.

relations.subject: vector-search:reranking
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: minted - requiresSetting. Reason: captures an index-creation-time configuration dependency (one setting only works if another setting was enabled at index-creation time), distinct in kind from requiresPrivilege/requiresEdition/requiresCapellaRole which are all about actor access rights, not index configuration state.
relations.evidence: You must have your index set to persist the full vector value, which increases memory use.

relations.subject: vector-search:train-list
relations.evidence: Tests show that increasing the `trainlist` improves QPS and reduces latency, but slightly increases memory usage for the index.

relations.subject: vector-search:replicas-setting
relations.evidence: Tests show that increasing the number of replicas linearly increases the QPS and linearly reduces the latency of queries that use the index. However, it also linearly increases the memory footprint of the index.

relations.subject: vector-search:partitions-setting
relations.evidence: Tests show that increasing the number of partitions linearly reduces both the time it takes to build and train the index and index's memory use.

relations.subject: vector-search:product-quantization
relations.evidence: Use PQ when you're willing to trade some accuracy for higher compression and less memory use. PQ is a good choice for larger datasets (millions to billions of vectors) where you want to reduce memory use and improve search performance.

relations.subject: n1ql:vector-distance
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused (promoted predicate) - context-specific: for recall-rate ground-truth measurement only, not for normal production queries (see the opposite-direction relation logged in hyperscale-vector-index.json for the production-query context)
relations.evidence: The `VECTOR_DISTANCE` function performs a brute-force full vector comparison, so it returns the most accurate results.

cross_component_finding: This page's guidance is explicitly framed as Hyperscale-first with a caveat that findings often (not always) transfer to Composite Vector indexes ('Most of the tests were performed using the Hyperscale Vector index... many of the results also apply to Composite Vector indexes where the two index types share the same settings') - but nList is called out as a case where the two index types respond in OPPOSITE directions (Composite wants larger nList for better QPS; Hyperscale wants smaller nList/larger centroids for better performance). This is a concrete example of sharesOptionSetWith (same setting name/mechanism) coexisting with behavesDifferentlyUnder (opposite tuning advice) for the same setting across two index types - worth the coordinator's attention since these two predicates are not mutually exclusive here.
